entries.title: The Growing Lawlessness in California’s Forests
entries.summary: Two frog biologists were kidnapped in the woods. More bizarre situations may come.
entries.content:
Two frog biologists were kidnapped in the woods. More bizarre situations may come.

On the day of the kidnapping, the campground at Gumboot Lake happened to be nearly empty, so Joseph Charles Henrichsen was one of the only people to see the two Forest Service biologists pull up in their pickup truck. Federal employees didn’t visit all that much—campers who’d been coming to the small alpine lake for years told me they’d never seen a ranger on patrol in these Northern California woods. But some of the regulars had noticed the “frog people,” as one called them, quietly collecting their specimens the previous summer. These particular biologists, both women, were there to survey the Cascades frog, whose well-being can help signal the health of the overall ecosystem.

People at Gumboot Lake tended to give one another space, but that July morning, Henrichsen approached the biologists as they worked. He was holding, authorities would later allege, an AR-15-style assault rifle, and told the biologists to turn around and put their hands in the air. He zip-tied their wrists behind their backs and ordered them to walk to his camping trailer, parked at a site strewn with crates and refuse, the clothesline heavy with towels. His 23-year-old son, Phoenix, made room for the biologists inside.

What Henrichsen’s intention was that day—what he thought he might achieve by abducting two government scientists, whether he had a clear motivation at all beyond an impulse of self-righteousness and a loaded gun—remains uncertain. Before long, he escorted one of the biologists back to their Forest Service truck. He drove several miles with her down a winding road along the Sacramento River. Glimpses of Mount Shasta, the volcano looming to the east, reared up through the trees. Along the way, he made calls, according to the FBI. He spoke with a Forest Service ranger and left a message with another person who has not been identified. “I’ve taken two Fed biologists hostage from the Forest Service,” he said, according to authorities. “What I’d like to have happen, I’d like to have you send me a fucking Fed investigator, with a goddamn badge, preferably from the FBI. And we can talk things through a little bit.”

Over the next few hours, Gumboot Lake and the surrounding Shasta-Trinity National Forest would swarm with law enforcement in helicopters and Bearcat armored vehicles. Local SWAT teams and snipers, then more than 50 FBI officers, poured into the national forest. A Boeing 757 flew across the country, from Virginia, with an elite FBI hostage-rescue team.

All of these officers were confronting a man who had a history of erratic behavior: Henrichsen had been released from a Washington State psychiatric hospital a few years before, after allegedly tormenting a neighbor by firing a gun, throwing fireworks on his porch, and placing zip-tie handcuffs on his property. But Henrichsen had also managed to stay at Gumboot Lake for months—well past the official seven-day limit—apparently without triggering any official response from the Forest Service. Many of the campsite’s regulars had crossed paths with the Henrichsens over the summer, and although Charles held himself apart, he struck them as a familiar type, not so out of place here among the free spirits and drifters living in their cars. That he’d turned out to be unhinged or anti-government enough to kidnap a couple of federal frog biologists didn’t seem to shock them. In fact, with the way things are going on the woolier fringes of America’s public lands, maybe something like this was bound to happen.

Siskiyou County, the area that includes Gumboot Lake, has a reputation for fierce independence and the hostility toward government meddling that often comes with it. The county leans conservative, though Mount Shasta is a magnet for a crunchier type: crystal enthusiasts, New Age spiritualists, pilgrims on the road to Burning Man. Hikers stream down the Pacific Crest Trail, which runs along a ridge above the lake. On Sundays, some of the campers at Gumboot Lake like to gather for a drum circle, and when the full moon arrives, people convene to celebrate.

The Gumboot Lake campground is free and has no assigned spots, no running water, limited cell signal, and a lone pit toilet. It’s one of dozens of alpine lakes in the Trinity Divide accessible by car or off-road vehicle. Others are more popular. The Forest Service described the campground in one write-up as a “typical meadow type lake, not very beautiful.” But it’s relatively easy to get to, just a 40-minute drive up from Interstate 5.

I made that drive last month, not long after the Forest Service had reopened Gumboot Lake, less than a week after the kidnapping. I saw old vans and school buses parked along the Forest Service road leading to the campsite; people had strung up hammocks between the trees. At the lake, several campers had already set up their tents and parked their mobile homes. One camper, a 24-year-old backpacker from Australia, told me the campsite was a place to “drop in with the land, drop in with each other, cook meals with each other, and just be super present.” As we talked, a large shirtless man, whom she called Zephyr, appeared and handed her a slice of papaya.

The Forest Service is supposed to be a steward of its public lands, preserving them while still allowing people to enjoy the woods and use their resources. Dispersed camping—outside of established campgrounds—is allowed in most national forests. And although people here are supposed to move on after seven nights, locals say that plenty of people live out of their cars for much longer. Informal settlements are widespread on the national-forest lands of Oregon and Northern California. People tend to cluster along the river corridors, most of them peaceable campers. “But the last 10 percent of them are pretty sad,” says Gabriel Howe, the executive director of the Siskiyou Mountain Club, a group that maintains trails and campgrounds in the region. “People living out there, people manufacturing drugs and all sorts of nasty stuff.”

Policing a remote forest is unlike any other job in law enforcement. The Shasta-Trinity spans more than 3,000 square miles, and the Forest Service is perennially under-resourced. Carmen Kinch, a Forest Service law officer who patrolled the area around Gumboot Lake in the late 1990s and 2000s, told me that back then, seven law-enforcement officers worked across the entire forest. Today, there are four. Not one, she said, is currently based in the Forest Service management unit that includes Gumboot Lake.

The drop in personnel is not just a problem in this one forest. Since last year, the Forest Service’s staffing across the country has fallen by about 20 percent as a result of firings and departures encouraged by the Trump administration, part of its push to reduce the federal workforce. In the Shasta-Trinity forest, excluding firefighting roles, the permanent staff—employees who maintain campsites and conduct wildlife research—has been reduced by about a quarter, one former U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the topic, told me. (Bob Doucette, a Forest Service spokesperson, told me that staffing levels are “similar” to what they’ve been in the past few years and said that “all employees continue to meet public needs.”) Howe has worked in the region for 15 years, and he sees the Forest Service as a slowly dying patient. “Around COVID, it went into palliative care, and now it’s on hospice,” he told me.

A sense of lawlessness seems to be growing on the public lands in the region. People on Howe’s staff have returned to find their cars stripped at trailheads—no wheels, no batteries, gas siphoned. They’ve encountered mountain roads blockaded by hostile civilians. Michael Kauffmann, an ecologist and the executive director of the Bigfoot Trail Alliance, told me that he’s recently instituted more training for his researchers and trail crews on safety measures and defusing confrontations. More than anything, Kauffmann has noticed a greater disregard for the rules—more graffiti, a lot more garbage, and less appreciation for these lands as places to care for rather than to joyride over with guns and four-wheelers. One person who regularly hikes in the area around Gumboot Lake told me that he’d felt safer during “close encounters with bears and lions” than with some of the armed and unfriendly people around.

The Henrichsens had apparently lived at Gumboot Lake since at least early May, when Todd Heie, another camper who visits the lake regularly, first encountered them. In early June, Joseph Charles Henrichsen, who goes by his middle name, asked a neighbor at the campground, Kevin Airoldi, for a lift into town. On the 45-minute drive, Charles said that he and his son were “just traveling around, trying to do it on the cheap.”

Charles mentioned that they’d come down from the Pacific Northwest but not what he’d left behind. He’d once been a successful mortgage-loan broker in Orange County, California. But he had run into business trouble, and his relationship with Phoenix’s mother had fallen apart. By 2022, he was divorced and living near Bellingham, Washington, up by the Canadian border. That year, he spent six months in a county jail, charged with a hate crime for allegedly harassing his neighbor. Police said that he “appeared to be spiraling in his mental health,” according to court documents. Henrichsen, who kept multiple guns at his home, would rant about world events, including the war in Ukraine; an evaluation found that he likely had schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder. Although a judge ordered him to be admitted to a hospital for psychiatric treatment, bureaucratic delays kept him out for months. Even then, he was admitted only briefly, after the charges had been dropped.

At Gumboot Lake, both Charles and Phoenix Henrichsen tended to keep to themselves in their Feather Ultra Lite trailer, parked amid the lodgepole pines. The other campers would watch them pacing around the lake, lap after lap, as the father appeared to loudly lecture, or preach, to the son, who kept his head down and rarely said a word. Many found Charles intense and standoffish. He would burn red sage during the day, and at night he would play a type of chanting Indian music that Heie, a former director of the county’s department of corrections, sometimes listened to as he drifted in his kayak, looking up at the sky. At one point, Aaron Sullivan, a software engineer who was working remotely out of a Winnebago along the lake, stopped by the Henrichsens’ campsite. He’d been impressed by Charles’s strong, lean frame and “big, beautiful beard.” Sullivan invited them to one of the full-moon gatherings. We won’t be doing that, Charles told him.

The Thursday morning of the kidnapping, on July 16, Charles Henrichsen must have been watching the biologists before he approached them—it’s unclear how long. After he had captured the women and herded one of them into the pickup truck, he kept her tightly restrained. He told the unidentified recipient of the message he left while driving down the mountain that “her hands are behind her fucking back, and I’ve got live rounds ready to fucking [inaudible] anyone who fucks with me,” according to the criminal complaint.

When Siskiyou County Sheriff Jeremiah LaRue was alerted to the situation that morning, he thought the man could be swatting, he told me—attempting to trick his office into scrambling to respond. His county is larger than Connecticut, and more than half of it is public land. Sheriff’s deputies soon arrived at Gumboot Lake to find the campsite gate closed and a gray Subaru blocking the road. (The Subaru, police would later learn, was stolen, possibly by the Henrichsens, and likely parked there to block others from entering during the kidnapping.) The sheriff’s deputies flew a drone overhead and quickly spotted the Forest Service truck that Henrichsen had commandeered, LaRue said. A man stepped out of the trailer, carrying a rifle, and later the deputies saw him with someone whose hands were bound. “He’s now pointing a rifle at the drone,” a deputy said over the radio. LaRue knew he had to get more people up there.

Police set up in a dirt roundabout on the north side of the lake, within shouting distance of Henrichsen’s trailer, where he had holed back up with Phoenix and both biologists; they blocked access to the campground, and law enforcement streamed in from California and elsewhere, their cars crowding the narrow Forest Service road. Hank Magnuski, a retired tech executive who owned a nearby cabin, came upon the pileup of armored vehicles and heavily armed agents in the early afternoon, at the end of a long drive from his home in Palo Alto. He was startled by the military-style occupation of this out-of-the-way wilderness, but he gave two SWAT-team members a ride up the road. “What’s the occasion?” he asked one of them.

At about 3:30 p.m, more than four hours after his initial calls, Henrichsen’s voice came over law-enforcement radio. He had taken one of the biologists back to their truck, where she helped him access the radio to contact the Forest Service’s dispatcher and the FBI. He seemed calm; he repeated his request to speak with FBI officials, “so I can release these hostages. Over.”

The reception was choppy enough that he started negotiating with the FBI agent Russell Quiniola about how they might speak in person. “Are you comfortable putting the rifle down and coming to a point where you feel safe?” Quiniola asked.

“Listen, you come and talk to me,” Henrichsen responded. “I would suggest coming unarmed, because if you have one, that might trigger something in me, you never know. Or you may have a rifle, and you see me, that might trigger something in you. But I suggest we get the show on the road. These ladies would like to go home. Over.”

The fact that Henrichsen had initiated contact with authorities by requesting to talk with the FBI was, to some degree, encouraging. It suggested that his intentions went beyond simply harming the biologists, Gary Noesner, a former chief of the FBI’s crisis-negotiation unit, told me. In such situations, every hour that negotiators can keep the kidnapper talking is one without violence. Unless they sense that the risk is increasing, Noesner said, “we’ll talk ’til the cows come home.”

Quiniola and other FBI agents spoke with Henrichsen over the next nine hours. By 1 a.m., the standoff had gone on so long with such little progress that LaRue was surprised when someone in his vehicle said, “One of the females is coming out,” and the first biologist opened the door of the trailer and walked toward the police. Her colleague followed six minutes later. Another hour and a half would pass, during which FBI agents exploded flash-bangs around the trailer—a commotion heard by hikers on the Pacific Crest Trail above the lake—before Phoenix and then Charles finally turned themselves over and the government vehicles lining the road to Gumboot Lake started heading back down the mountain.

By the time I arrived at the lake, almost all signs that this place had been the site of such force were gone. The Henrichsens’ trailer had been towed away; their debris had been bagged and left in the outhouse, along with a note that read, “Trash from the kidnappers campsite.” One camper had held on to three wooden billy clubs found amid the mess. I set up my tent at a campsite next to the Henrichsens’, where I could see the lake through the pines. Everything was serene. The day was cloudless, and the sun sparkled on the water.

Charles and Phoenix Henrichsen eventually pleaded not guilty in federal court in Sacramento to charges of kidnapping federal employees and other felony counts that carry the prospect of life in prison. Charles’s lead defense attorney, Mia Crager, told me that her client had intended no harm to the biologists; according to police, the two women, who have not been named publicly, did not appear to suffer major injuries during their 15 hours as hostages. “What happened on July 16 was preventable and resulted from system failures on a number of levels,” Crager said in a statement. She did not elaborate on the type of failures she was referring to, and didn’t respond to questions about any specific allegations against Hendrichsen. She said that Charles “hopes that some good will come of the case, including that his son Phoenix will get the mental health care he sorely needs.”

Phoenix’s lawyer, Kresta Daly, told me that Phoenix had been an unwilling participant in the standoff: He had no gun, didn’t know what was going to happen, and, once the crisis had started, he hoped that it would resolve peacefully. His main thought, Daly said, was “How do I stop anyone from dying today, me included?” His father, Daly told me, had hurt him before; he’d been in the hospital earlier this summer after Charles beat him up. Charles Henrichsen, through his lawyers, did not respond to questions about that accusation, but agreed that his son “was not at all at fault for what happened that day, nor was he an active participant.”

Henrichsen’s specific demands during the hostage crisis have not yet been fully explained. He did not leave a manifesto. An FBI spokesperson declined to describe those hours of discussions with Henrichsen, citing the ongoing investigation. Sheriff LaRue, who had been inside a Bearcat with the FBI negotiators during part of the process, said he couldn’t hear Henrichsen “discussing anything as to why he was doing this, what his motives were.” At least in that moment, he seemed to want the attention of the federal government. He got it.

The day of the biologists’ release, the chief of the Forest Service, Tom Schultz, wrote an email to agency staff expressing his gratitude to law enforcement and his support for the two women after their ordeal. A safety manager with the agency followed up the next week, with links to security tips and videos with titles such as “Avoiding Trouble” and “Building Trust in Small Towns.” Despite such internal gestures, some former Forest Service leaders heard little public support for the staff from an administration that has shed civil servants without much remorse. “There’s not an ounce of empathy for federal employees,” Vicki Christiansen, a former chief of the Forest Service during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, told me. “Not an ounce.”

As I talked with people at the lake, the hostage episode began to seem inseparable from the deepening neglect of our country’s public lands. Whatever the Henrichsens’ personal motives may have been, the erosion of day-to-day management has made ruptures in the fragile relations among strangers in the woods all the more likely. “They shouldn’t be letting someone stay here for months on end,” Heie, the former corrections officer, told me. In the early evening, I watched him paddle his kayak to the middle of the lake. Another man stood in the shallows, casting a fishing line. Through the trees, I heard a couple laughing. I kept looking around at the peaceful scene, unable to shake the unsettling feeling that something was off. As darkness settled, I sat in my camping chair, listening for the sounds of the frogs.

entries.title: Hegseth’s Pentagon Lurches off the Rails
entries.summary: The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is the latest sign of severe dysfunction in the Defense Department.
entries.content:
The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is the latest sign of severe dysfunction in the Defense Department.

Making Pete Hegseth the secretary of defense was always a huge gamble. A television host with little background in national-security or defense affairs, who topped out as a major in the National Guard, he was nominated based on the same qualification shared by most of Donald Trump’s other appointees: loyalty. And now the price of that gamble is evident. The Pentagon is careening offtrack under a secretary of defense who is firing or forcing the resignations of officers and civilian officials, not because they are unqualified but because he believes they are insufficiently loyal to him, personally.

The latest casualty of Hegseth’s ongoing purge is Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned today after repeatedly clashing with the secretary of defense. As my colleagues Nancy A. Youssef, Missy Ryan, and Michael Scherer report, a person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation said that he had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” In the careful circumlocutions of Washington-speak, that means that Driscoll went to the White House to complain about Hegseth, and the president sided with Hegseth.

But more issues were in play than “Army transformation.” Hegseth’s tenure has been disastrous on multiple scores. Instead of giving sound advice to the commander in chief and ensuring that America remains secure while the president fights a deeply unwise war of choice, he has been pursuing his political grievances about DEI and other pet peeves against the U.S. military. Hegseth seems to have a special animus toward the Army, an institution he claims “spit me out.” He fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, and he has pushed out other senior Army officers; at this point, the Army has no Senate-confirmed chief of staff or secretary. (George’s replacement, General Christopher LaNeve, so far does not have the necessary votes to be confirmed.)

Even in less dangerous times, Hegseth’s irresponsible behavior would be a hazard to American national security. The Defense Department is a huge bureaucracy; it requires a leader who understands more than the mechanics of teaching trainees how to do push-ups or how to handle a weapon. Secretaries of defense must grasp the economics of the defense industry, the nature of alliances, congressional politics, the policy process, and dozens of other issues for which Hegseth seems to care little and about which he knows even less.

In a time of war, however, Hegseth’s shortcomings may prove deadly. Leave aside his early stumbles, including the mishandling of sensitive information. Leave aside, even, that Hegseth dissembled about the severity of Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf that had succeeded in disrupting the logistical support for American forces in the theater and led to the kind of deprivations that were suffered by the crew of the aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln. Hegseth’s incompetence, and his commitment to staying in Trump’s good graces, helped launch the war itself in the first place.

Hegseth was reportedly virtually alone among senior officials in supporting Trump’s decision to attack Iran—when he should have been the one person in the room who knew better. The secretary of state and CIA director were against the idea. According to the The Wall Street Journal, even then–Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, another of Trump’s unqualified-but-sycophantic appointees, mustered the courage to give the president bad news, telling Trump that killing the reigning ayatollah and striking Iran would “likely usher in a more hard-line regime open to acquiring nuclear weapons”; that the Iranians “would rush to close the Strait of Hormuz, destabilizing the global energy market”; and that Iran “would strike U.S. forces and partners in the Middle East,” all of which happened almost immediately after Trump gave the order to go to war.

Hegseth, however, supported Trump’s fantasies of a quick victory. A man of principle would have warned his president even at the risk of his job, but Pete Hegseth is not that man.

And now Hegseth has banished another enemy, Driscoll, from the Pentagon. But as the saying goes: Play stupid games, win stupid prizes. Hegseth, more than ever, now owns every aspect of the Pentagon’s dysfunction. Yesterday, The Washington Post reported that multiple senior military leaders—those still left, that is—have warned Hegseth that the United States cannot indefinitely extend military operations against Iran. Even the chief of naval operations, Admiral Darryl Caudle (who campaigned for the job by signaling his agreement with the secretary’s culture-war obsessions), told Hegseth that the Navy cannot “sustain its current level of support for the Iran conflict because there is no anticipated end date.”

Hegseth’s response to this story was to send his spokespeople out to castigate the press for revealing classified information. In an amateurish bungle, the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said that the reports were “inaccurate” but also a “betrayal of the force”—leading sensible people to ask how the stories could be false and dangerous at the same time. And these were just the responses from people who are officially authorized to speak for the Pentagon; another bombshell report over the weekend revealed that the department has recruited online influencers into paid roles, but without either the influencers or the Pentagon telling anyone about their cozy arrangement with the government.

Hegseth, meanwhile, has dutifully overseen the raiding of assets from other theaters to support Trump’s war with Iran, leaving the U.S. and its allies exposed to potential threats from China and Russia. When Trump returned to office, Hegseth and others supported a reorientation away from the Middle East and Europe. Now the secretary and the other supposed China hawks have discarded those positions and dumped everything into a war that still has no clear strategy and no clear goal beyond stopping Iran from attaining a nuclear weapon it didn’t have in the first place.

Fortunately, even under the strain of a petty and incompetent secretary, and a president mired in his delusions, senior military officers are still speaking up and telling their boss the truth about America’s parlous defense situation. One of the advantages of a large bureaucracy staffed with professionals is that much of it can run and function, at least for a while, under even the most inept leaders.

But Hegseth is apparently close to getting the Pentagon he wants: Much like his boss at the White House, Hegseth seems to desire a building full of loyalists who put the boss’s personal fortunes over the national interest. Some reports indicate, for example, that Hegseth wants to replace Driscoll with Parnell—who has no significant qualifications for the post beyond his time fighting with the press on the secretary’s behalf.

The result of all this is that the United States is losing a war to a third-rate power in the Middle East. The Russians, meanwhile, are continuing their rampage in Europe and apparently considering things so perilous that the CIA director had to fly to Moscow just to warn the Kremlin off of whatever it was thinking of doing. The Chinese are watching as Trump and Hegseth have stripped the Pacific theater of its only American aircraft carrier. In the midst of this chaos, Hegseth does chin-ups while he ponders calling all of America’s admirals and generals back to another mass meeting so he can again carp at them about fat soldiers and bearded sailors.

Pete Hegseth has failed in every mission except one: keeping his job. But firing or forcing out everyone else in the Pentagon will not make Pete Hegseth into the secretary of defense America and its men and women in uniform need. With each dismissal, he exposes only his own insecurities, even as he manages to stay employed—but the people and the armed forces of the United States are paying the inevitable price of his incompetence.

entries.title: Dan Driscoll’s Parting Shot
entries.summary: The Army secretary told Trump about problems in the Army and his friction with Hegseth, then resigned.
entries.content:
The Army secretary told Trump about problems in the Army and his friction with Hegseth, then resigned.

During a White House meeting last week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll brought his concerns about the future of the Army under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directly to President Trump—a sign of how far tensions between the two Pentagon leaders had escalated, and of the dysfunction inside the building, four people familiar with the conversation told us.

Trump was surprised when Driscoll told him how many generals and other top officers had been fired, pushed out, or passed over for promotion under Hegseth, one of the people said. Driscoll argued that the Army could not transform itself the way it needs to, because of the departure of so many leaders, this person said, adding that Trump expressed concern about the deep cuts to the Army’s senior leadership. Driscoll informed the president of his intention to resign—and by today, Driscoll was on his way out.

Hegseth’s purge of the military has been so dramatic that with Driscoll gone, the military’s largest service is left without a top civilian leader, a Senate-confirmed top general, a confirmed Army general in charge of operations, or a confirmed commander of Army troops in Europe. Because of all the firings across the service over the past year, the Army, with more than 450,000 active-duty soldiers positioned across the globe, has fewer generals than at any point in recent history. Driscoll’s personal appeal to Trump just days before his exit was the most direct articulation of high-level concerns among Pentagon leaders about the strains facing the force—including Hegseth’s intervention in Army personnel decisions and the mounting demands of the Iran war.

The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Driscoll had been “highly effective” in improving soldier readiness and advancing other administration priorities. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” Kelly wrote in a statement, using the administration’s preferred term for the Department of Defense.

Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment, and Driscoll did not respond to a call seeking comment. But a person familiar with his resignation told us that Driscoll had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” Hegseth did not have an immediate response to Driscoll’s departure.

Since his arrival at the Pentagon early last year, Hegseth—a former Fox News host who appealed to Trump loyalists by deriding a “woke” military and advocating for leniency for troops charged with war crimes—has sought to reshape the Army. He has placed like-minded generals in positions of influence, intervened to stymie the promotions of lower ranking-officers, and gutted diversity initiatives. The result was an Army depleted of leaders, and an Army secretary and a Pentagon chief at constant odds. Hegseth has ended dozens of Army careers, all without any clear explanation. He now has driven out the secretary of the Army.

Driscoll’s departure puts the Pentagon even more firmly under the control of Hegseth and his MAGA agenda. Driscoll is a confidant of Vice President Vance, a relationship that gave him access to the West Wing, and at times Driscoll served as a counterweight to Hegseth’s impulses, but only up to a point. Some current and former defense officials told us they believe Driscoll’s enmity toward Hegseth actually had the unintended consequence of broadening the purge of the uniformed ranks. And yet Driscoll’s departure, which had been expected for months, and the prospect that he will be replaced by someone more politically aligned with Hegseth are already raising fears inside the Army. “What happens then? Generational damage,” a defense official told us.

Driscoll arrived at the Pentagon in February 2025, a third-generation Army soldier who shared several things in common with Hegseth, his new boss. Like Hegseth, Driscoll joined the military in the most muscular years of Washington’s post-9/11 wars. Both men served in Iraq in a company-grade role. (Hegseth, a National Guardsman, also deployed to Afghanistan.) Both returned with sharp criticisms of America’s overseas adventures and the military’s hidebound ways. Both attended Ivy League schools: Hegseth, Princeton and Harvard; Driscoll, Yale Law, where he befriended the fellow veteran Vance. Both Driscoll and Hegseth have made unsuccessful runs for political office. Both have also eyed a return to politics. As Army secretary, Driscoll frequently reminded people that he had a direct line to the vice president, people familiar with the matter said, and told others that he had ambition to someday run for president himself—an ambition that Hegseth is also said to harbor.

But the two men differed starkly in temperament and style. Hegseth, who required an unprecedented tie-breaking Senate-confirmation vote from Vance after failing to win any Democratic support, is one of Trump’s most reliable MAGA warriors. He has publicly boasted about firing “woke” generals, dared military dissenters to quit, and demonized the mainstream media. Driscoll also supported administration policies but has done so in a more genial way that appealed to many lawmakers more than Hegseth’s combative approach before Congress. And unlike Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who has echoed Hegseth’s scornful and partisan tone on social media, Driscoll has steered clear of endorsing Hegseth’s most controversial actions or most of his culture-war priorities. Unlike Hegseth, Driscoll is friendly with the press, cultivated ties with lawmakers of both parties, and courted technology leaders as he promoted the Army’s sprint to transform how it wages war. That served him well in the administration, earning him additional responsibilities as director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and later as an unofficial mediator for the war in Ukraine. None of that sat well with Hegseth.

Army personnel appointments were a particular point of friction. Hegseth has not hesitated to push aside or promote officers as he sees fit, in many cases in ways that have irked others in the Pentagon. Driscoll advocated for General Randy George, the Army chief of staff whose name appeared on a list circulated before Trump’s return to office of senior officers who should be fired due to perceived transgressions against the MAGA agenda. Although Driscoll may have bought George time, Hegseth ultimately fired the general in April. Chris Donahue, the four-star general who headed U.S. Army Europe and Africa, followed several months later.

The Army has been without a top commander since George’s firing. General Christopher LaNeve, who was picked by Hegseth as the No. 2 officer in the Army, has been acting in that role, often going straight to Hegseth for decisions, bypassing Driscoll, according to defense officials. Hegseth is expected to nominate LaNeve to lead the Army, but Capitol Hill is already signaling that LaNeve would struggle to be confirmed, because of many lawmakers’ antipathy to Hegseth. “We are not going to reward Hegseth for what he did to the Army,” one congressional staffer told us.

The Army has long prided itself on representing the diversity of the country, but under Hegseth, minorities and women have been pushed out or barred from promotion. The military has long sought to be apolitical, but under Hegseth, troops are measured not by combat experience but by their perceived loyalty to the administration. Among the generals fired have been some of the most experienced and decorated in the service. Each departure marks the loss of decades of investment in that soldier and raises questions about how future troops can rise through the ranks.

Although Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the near term, many Pentagon officials fear that the administration will nominate the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, another Army veteran, to replace Driscoll. Parnell, who previously made a failed bid for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania, shares Hegseth’s pugilistic spirit and interest in culture and personnel issues. Like Hegseth, Parnell has no experience managing a large organization and would face a contentious confirmation hearing. A new Army secretary who is more politically driven—and likely less experienced and less well connected than Driscoll—could keep the service embroiled in cultural fights rather than focused on the long-term planning that Driscoll and others believe it desperately needs.

entries.title: Trump’s Economy Goes to the Polls
entries.summary: Trump wants Republicans to run on his record in the midterms. Democrats do as well.
entries.content:
Trump wants Republicans to run on his record in the midterms. Democrats do as well.

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the policies of the party in power; President Trump is hoping that Republicans steer into the skid. Last week, my colleagues reported that the president—dogged by the war in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and an economy that has Americans dipping into their savings for groceries and daily expenses—hopes that Republicans seeking to win reelection or gain seats will use his time in office to sway voters.

But that strategy could play directly into the hands of Democrats hoping to take back both chambers of Congress. My colleagues the Atlantic staff writers Michael Scherer and Ashley Parker join me this week to discuss Congress, the economy, and the midterm elections.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Ashley Parker: At the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent.

[Music]

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and this week, we need to think about the midterms.

The House of Representatives is back on Capitol Hill this week as the nation turns its attention to the general election. It’s the last opportunity for lawmakers to show they are working for their constituents.

Meanwhile, President Trump is trying to convince congressional Republicans to run on his record. But amid a war with Iran driving up the price of everyday items and a burgeoning trade war with Canada, Americans are feeling the pinch of the president’s agenda.

And Democrats, on the heel of bitter primary races around the country, are hoping to seize upon the president’s unpopularity, and they’re banking that Americans want something different. The question is: Are they right? I’m joined by my colleagues Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer to discuss.

Ashley, Michael, welcome to the show.

Michael Scherer: Thanks for having us.

Parker: Thanks for having us.

Harris: Ashley, I want to start with you first. Congress is back this week, and one of the first things that they must do is to fund the government, right? Do you think that Congress is more likely to get this done in a timely manner than we’ve seen in some of these previous spending cycles?

Parker: Yeah, I mean, a lot of these stopgap measures end up being incredibly fraught and going up to the last minute. This one is looking like it’s going to be less controversial, in part because what House members really wanna do is get back to their districts to campaign for the midterms. And so there’s a few things in there that might raise some eyebrows, but the sense right now is that they’ll be able to, they hope, push this through pretty quickly.

Harris: Speaking of kind of getting back to the districts for the midterms, right, this is a very important cycle. I feel like every cycle we say, It’s, you know—

Scherer: —most important election of your lifetime.

Harris: Exactly. The most important one of the lifetime. But this one is a pretty important cycle, particularly for Democrats hoping to stop the president’s agenda and for Republicans hoping to continue with the president’s policies moving forward.

Oftentimes, parties don’t like to make this a referendum on the presidency. I’m reminded of [Barack] Obama saying, I’m not on the ballot, but these policies are certainly on the ballot.

And you both have reported that Trump is planning to roll out a series of TV ads that are touting his personal record leading up to the midterms in November. What does this ad blitz say about the administration and how they’re feeling about the election prospects, Michael, and the president’s image?

Scherer: Yeah, so there’s a formula for midterm elections. It’s always a referendum on those in power. So the in-party—the people who hold the presidency, and if they also hold the House, the Senate—try their best to make it a choice, not a referendum, to basically put the opposing party in the spotlight, say, Look, they’re terrible and bad and have done all these awful things, and if you give them back power, it’ll be terrible. And they’re always fighting an uphill battle, because voters don’t see it that way, and voters tend to just, you know, say, I’m happy or I’m pissed off. And you know, for the last four decades, they’re almost always pissed off when it comes to a midterm.

This cycle is a little different because of voting patterns and the appeal of President Trump.

[It] used to be that Republicans turned out more than Democrats in midterms. Now that’s kind of reversed. Democrats are more likely to turn out in midterms. [It] used to be that presidents don’t really have much impact on who turns out in midterms, for the reasons I just said—you know, it’s a referendum, and people are upset. Republicans are betting on this idea that their biggest problem is motivation, that they have the voters out there, that if they can get those voters to the polls, they can stem their losses, they could actually overperform expectations.

But the polls right now show, you know, they’re not that excited. Like, a Fox News poll a few weeks ago asked, Are you extremely motivated to vote? Democrat voters were like 70 percent saying they’re extremely motivated; Republican voters, like 60 percent saying they were extremely motivated. And so the White House solution to that, the president’s solution to that, is to say, We’ve got the magic man on the stump here. We’re going to make this about President Trump, which really undermines the pattern I just described. You know, the Republicans and the Democrats now are in some way saying, We’re gonna make this a referendum on the president.

Parker: And to be clear, everything is always about President Trump. That’s just the rule of President Trump. And so as much as this strategy that Michael and I and our colleague Yvonne reported last week seems counterintuitive and is legitimately frustrating to some Republicans, the White House thinking and the president’s thinking is, It’s always about Trump, right?

And he likes it being about himself, and so if it’s gonna be about him, we might as well put him front and center and tout what we believe are his accomplishments.

Harris: Yeah, if he’s gonna be there, why run away from him? Might as well steer into the skid, right?

Scherer: The problem is that the more you’re talking about Trump and trying to convince people that he’s, you know, improved everyone’s lives when the polls show people don’t feel like he’s improved their lives in the last year and a half, the less you’re talking about Democrats.

And so, you know, that’s the choice they’re making. It’s not that it’s a terrible idea to be talking about the president.

You know, another pattern is, like, Obama would go out on the stump and, you know, [Joe] Biden went on the stump in his midterm elections, [George W. ] Bush went on the stump in his midterm elections, and would obviously talk about their own records. So it’s not like presidents don’t talk about themselves. The difference here is putting money on TV and digital media about the president.

Normally, the in-party only wants to talk about how terrible and bad the out-party is. And, you know, that’s especially true for super PACs. The president’s talking about spending. He’s got $400 million we know about. He may have hundreds of millions more in sort of dark money, basically independent money he’s collected. Normally, that money is just used to ravage the other side and just tear them apart. And the idea that the president’s gonna put some significant part of that behind convincing people that no tax on tips, or the stock-market highs, or the closed border have really done them well is what’s so controversial.

Harris: And how are congressional Republicans feeling about this? How have they sort of responded to the president trying to have his name sort of be more forward in the campaign?

Parker: In general, if they’re speaking candidly, which they don’t really do in public, because they’re fearful of the blowback from President Trump, they find him generally unhelpful in this moment, right? A lot of the things he says and does just further the sense that he and his party don’t care about voters like them.

So there’s some stuff he said. He was recently at a rally in South Carolina for Darline Graham, Lindsay Graham’s sister, who’s running to replace him, where he said, I know my economic numbers are bad, but they should actually be at 100 percent. I’m doing such a great job. That makes people—who, you know, are going to maybe two or three grocery stores right now to use their coupons to get the best deals on what they can—feel like, He has no idea what my life is like. That’s, like, a very clear one where he’s talking about the economy.

But some of his other favorite topics are the ballroom, the new construction of the helipad on the South Lawn. And among all the various controversies that Trump has, these are physical, tangible things that voters really latch on to that Trump loves to talk about. At his core, it’s, like, cool to be president, but he’s sort of more animated by being a developer, you know, and a construction magnate. And so when he is talking about the marbling or the gilding or the slope of the helipad, even though that has nothing to do with the economy, that’s sort of the problem. That reminds voters, Look, this guy is focused on things for himself and his rich friends that again have nothing to do with me.

So Republicans privately will say, This is a nightmare. But at the end of the day, he’s their president, he’s what they’ve got. They know now, in sort of our 12th, 13th year of Trump, he’s not gonna change, and so this is the landscape they live in.

Scherer: And the biggest issue right now is not what the president is saying; it’s what the president has done. He won election very clearly in ’24 on the idea that he would lower prices and sort of reverse the economic squeeze that had emerged under Biden. And if you go back to February, March, White House was saying, like, This is how we’re gonna message this. This is our plan: Gas prices are down; interest rates are down; homeownership’s more affordable; generally, prices, inflation is stabilizing and dipping down.

All that’s been reversed by the Iran war. And so the biggest issue is not what the president’s saying or not saying. It’s that on Sunday night, the U.S. again had kinetic strikes against Iran. And we talked to a bunch of Republicans last week, and every one of them said, Well, it’s gonna be okay because we’re gonna have less actual violence in the Middle East over the next couple months. Every time another bomb goes off in the Middle East, it’s a hit to Republicans at this point.

Parker: And which, by the way, Michael is talking about the president promising to lower prices. His other big promise was no more foreign wars, right? So the thing that is contributing to prices is another very clear broken promise.

Harris: Well, I wanted to ask: What are hearing about the administration’s strategy, current strategy in the war, right? As you mentioned, Michael, the bombings resumed over the weekend. Are we actually trying to get out of this war, and how are Republicans up for reelection talking to their constituents about it?

Scherer: What the White House and the political advisers want is basically a cease of violence right now for the next couple months. I mean, that’s their desire, and they want to keep squeezing the Iranians. The Iranians are not in a great position economically, so they can keep squeezing them. The problem is the Iranians have enormous leverage on Trump, as we’ve just been describing. And the Iranian position is: We control the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. position is: You don’t control the Strait of Hormuz. So there’s, like, this deadlock at the center of the conflict. So every time, you know, the Iranians re-mine the Gulf or fire at another ship and the U.S. feels tempted to retaliate, it’s undermining the strategy the president has. And right now, the president doesn’t have control over that.

Harris: When we come back, Ashley and Michael on the burgeoning trade war with Canada and the Democrats chances in the midterm elections.

[Music]

Harris: So, Ashley, we have this actual war with Iran, but we also have this developing trade war with Canada. And it feels like the culmination of something that Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, said in January at Davos about the ways that countries with smaller economies needed to start renegotiating and looking out for themselves a little bit more. And there’s been a lot of tension between him and President Trump.

But I guess the thing that I keep coming back to with this trade war with Canada is: How did we end up back here? Why are we in this trade war with Canada?

Parker: Well, it’s the South Park truism of “Blame Canada,” right? Like, it’s just an easy thing to know. I mean, Trump likes tariffs. That’s clear and that’s true. And he’s very frustrated with Canada, in part because, as he said, you know, on the one hand, he’s sort of ready to get to trade-war footing with our neighbor to the north, and on the other hand, he’d happily make Canada a 51st state.

But therein is kind of the rub. If you hear Trump talk about it, he sort of says, Canada is getting all of the advantages of being a state, right? We’re subsidizing them to the tune of $200 billion. That’s not an accurate number, but that is what he says. And the thing that bothers Trump more than anything else is sort of, in his view, when people are taking advantage of him, profiting off of him. And, you know, that goes to, you know, former aides writing best-selling books from their time in the White House, to countries he believes sort of should be showing more deference to the United States than they are.

And then on the flip side, you mentioned Mark Carney’s speech to Davos, where he said what we’ve been hearing publicly a bit, and especially privately from a lot of our other especially European allies, which is: Originally, after Trump’s first term, they sort of thought it was, like, a fever dream that they could PTSD black out when Biden returned to the scene. And I remember going on Biden’s first foreign trip—I can’t remember if it was like a G7 or a G20—but that was literally his message. It was like, America, the America you know, the America you love; we’re back.

And then when Trump came back to power, the view, especially from our allies, was like, Maybe Biden was the aberration, right? And even though we know, you know, allegedly Trump was not gonna run for a third term, like, the allies’ thinking is, We have no idea if a new Trump, if a J. D. Vance, or if a populist on the Democrats’ side is gonna come in. And we kind of have to—we can’t count on the U.S., and these tacit deals we used to make with the U.S. (and by that I don’t mean a trade deal, but sort of that, like, We show deference to the United States because they are a bigger, more powerful, and ultimately benevolent force in the world)—we’re willing to take that; we’re willing to subjugate ourselves a bit.

They’ve decided, like, We’re not gonna do that anymore. So you also have a changing stance from our allies being much more willing to stand up for the United States and say, like, I’m not gonna bend my knee, because I can’t count on the United States. And by the way, I could agree to the worst trade terms with this president possible, and that might only placate him until his next Truth Social post.

Harris: Yeah, you know, actually, to that point of sort of the deference that was shown, we’ve also seen the ways that the president has sort of out-and-out attacked allied nations in recent weeks, from South Korea, thinking about some of the threats towards places like Oman.

And these aren’t small things, right? Even the fact that you mentioned something like the president saying that he’s not gonna run for a third term—to even to even think about a third term is sort of moving into an uncharted territory. Where does that leave the sort of long-term view of American responsibility as a world player?

Scherer: I mean, I think everybody’s just waiting out Trump to see what happens next. And I think what you’ve seen in Canada is their conclusion. I mean, exactly how that fell apart is, you know, there’s conflicting stories. But it does seem pretty clear that Canada views its maximum point of leverage as being right now. I mean, if they threaten to withhold electricity from the United States before midterm elections, that obviously it could have huge impacts on Trump. If they threaten to withhold electricity in early January, when Trump’s a lame duck, it may not have the same import.

I think the rest of the world is just coping with Trump. I mean, he’s so unpredictable. We don’t know how the last two years of his term will go. There’s just been a lot of preparation around the world to figure out how to reorient their own, you know, foreign policy to not depend on the U.S. going forward.

Harris: Yeah, we’ve talked about Republicans. I want to talk about the Democrats for just a moment. And Ashley, you’ve done some reporting on the Democrats and how they’re thinking about the midterms.

How much does the infighting of the primary, sort of the bitterness of the campaigns between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens in Michigan, races in Wisconsin, Florida, Maine, et cetera, sort of matter now to Democrats? And do Republicans sort of see an offset with the unpopularity of the president and the sort of discord that they might see among the Democrats?

Parker: I mean, it’s not helpful, right? One thing, when you talk about these races and you talk to people on both sides, and it’s always true, it’s like it’s a national referendum, but at the end of the day, candidates matter, districts matter, the dynamics of states matter, right? And so, you know, Susan Collins is someone who has great name recognition in Maine, fits the state very well. I’ve talked to Democrats who don’t vote for her, but they’ve told me, they’ve been like, I have to say, she has amazing constituent services, right? You know, when I was DOGEd, like, she was in constant contact with me.

And so, you know, for a state like that, or in Michigan, right, like, if you’re the Democrats, you want the best possible candidate for a general election. And there’s a sense among Democrats and Republicans that in some of these states and districts, they’ve done that, and in some of these states and districts, because of contentious primaries, they haven’t. That’s the first thing.

And it’s interesting: Republicans in many ways should be doing even worse than they seem poised to do, and when you kind of drill down on that a bit, one of the things you hear is, at the end of the day, every election is a choice, right? And Democrats have a pretty bad brand, universally.

Someone even said to me, Look, people don’t like the economy right now, what they’re feeling. And voters have short-term memories, but they still remember the Biden economy. And Democrats, again, individual candidates are doing things that are very compelling. But as a party, if I asked you, What is the Democratic Party plan to make this economic pinch better, to lower inflation, to cut prices?, almost no voter could tell you, because there doesn’t seem to be a bite-size talking point, cohesive, catchy, snappy Democratic plan.

Harris: People have pushed back against sloganeering and things like that, but not having a sort of digestible plan, not sort of having that digestible slogan, can also be an issue for voters who don’t necessarily see the big picture, right?

’Cause if you say, Well, we have a policy for supplemental nutrition benefits, and then we also have a policy for this and for this, it doesn’t sort of capture an economic picture. So how much does that sloganeering matter?

Parker: It’s Already I’m asleep, right?

Harris: Yeah.

Parker: I was talking to someone who runs focus groups among swing voters, and this person told me, You know, in a lot of these states, they will hold up the picture of the two Senate candidates running against each other in an election that’s now two months from now, and the voters can’t identify who either candidate is. And I don’t say that—I’m not making fun of voters. It’s a reality that like people are dealing with other things, right? Including the high cost.

So if you don’t even know the names of the candidates, the idea that you’re gonna remember like the third policy platform of an economic plan, it has to be something that—and I get the sloganeering and this kind of cheesiness about that. But at the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent. To dream.

Harris: Yeah. Michael, Republicans have a lot of money going into this election. How are they spending it? Sort of putting the president’s TV ads aside, how are they currently spending that money, and will that have an effect, right? Will that matter?

Scherer: Yeah, normally, the last decade or so, Democrats go into midterms, even they go into presidentials, with pretty substantial financial advantages. This is reversed this time. You know, by some estimates, if the president spent all the money he’s raised—and there’s a lot of dark money we can just estimate; we don’t really know—you’re talking about a $600 million to $1 billion advantage on the Republican side.

We know there’ll be a couple hundred million that will be spent because these are in the congressional and the Senate committees and in the campaign committees. We don’t know what the president’s gonna spend. We know that they plan to spend something. We know some portion of what they spend will be on ads defending the president’s record. But, you know, the president said in a recent interview that he had, I think, $850 million. We don’t have that on documents; we don’t know if that’s true. But if that’s true and he decides to spend all of it, that could be enormously impactful in a race like this.

I think it’s more likely he doesn’t spend all of it. I think the chance he can re-raise that amount of money in his last two years of office are pretty slim, and he probably wants to continue to have leverage over the party going forward, going into the next presidential race. So there’s a lot of speculation.

What is also very clear is: They have not done the typical thing you do when you have a huge financial advantage, which is to go up early and spend money in the spring or, you know, even in the summer to sort of lay the groundwork when your opponents can’t afford to be up on the air, you kind of have the airwaves to yourself. They haven’t done that, really. So there’s a lot of suspense, I think, about how that’s actually going to play out in the final months.

Harris: I’m gonna ask both of you to sort of open your reporter’s notebooks and think about sort of the threads that you’re going to be following this week. So, Ashley, I’m gonna go to you first. Sort of open your notebook. What are you thinking about in this week ahead?

Parker: Sure, I mean, I alluded to it a bit before, but the bottom, by all accounts, should have fallen out for Republicans in this midterm cycle. Just the historical headwinds of a midterm election with an incumbent president, how that normally goes: An economic referendum when people feel the economy is not doing well; when the president and his party control the White House, both chambers of Congress; when voters don’t like the president’s approval numbers; and especially for this president in particular, who sort of sold himself not entirely accurately as a as a businessman; when his economic numbers are underwater for the first time.

And so one thing I think Michael and I together are going to be looking at is—and again, it’s not that Republicans are supposed to do fantastically well, but there is a sense that, sort of generically, they should be doing worse than it looks like they’re going to be poised to do, which is: It looks like they’re probably gonna lose the House, lose their majority, but not by a ton. And the Senate is gonna be a real squeaker, which they may hold; Democrats may win, but it’ll be super tight. So trying to get into: Why are Republicans, even with gas prices what they are in August approaching an election, still sort of managing to barely hang on?

Harris: And Michael, same question to you.

Scherer: Another thing Ashley and I’ve been looking at is Cabinet travel. The president’s actually been—the White House’s been pretty good at deploying people around the country in a rather organized and sensible fashion. And then I’ve been working on a story about the sort of under-the-radar battle between the U.S. and Iran over decapitation assassination threats, which has sort of been, like, a weird current from the start of this conflict—where we started the war with Israel taking out most of the leadership of Iran, and continues now to, you know, there’s billboards all over Tehran now with the faces of the president’s family calling for their assassination, bounties on members of the administration and the family. So I’m looking at that as well.

Harris: Well, there will be a lot to look at in the week and months ahead as we run up to the midterms. Thank you both for helping us understand it better, and thanks for joining the show today.

Scherer: Yeah, thank you.

Parker: Thank you for having us.

[Music]

Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli. It was edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, you can subscribe to Radio Atlantic on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple, or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

entries.title: Trump’s Hatred of Free Speech Is Intensifying
entries.summary: The president’s latest attacks on Americans’ press freedom are dangerous, unconstitutional—and maybe self-defeating.
entries.content:
The president’s latest attacks on Americans’ press freedom are dangerous, unconstitutional—and maybe self-defeating.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Desensitization is one of Donald Trump’s most powerful tools: Through repetition, he acclimates Americans to troubling and dangerous ideas. Occasionally, though, his statements and actions are so outrageous that they can still provide a shock. The president’s hostility toward the media is familiar, but this weekend provided a clear reminder that Trump hates freedom of the press and will use any government power at his disposal to try to get rid of it.

Yesterday morning, Trump started off with a post on Truth Social demanding that the Federal Communications Commission do something about “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA.” About 15 minutes later, he followed this with a long rant about Kristen Welker of Meet the Press, complaining that she had noted that Trump’s record in recent endorsements had been “a mixed bag.” Along with some casual misogyny, Trump wrote, “How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

The reasons for Trump’s anger are plain: Polls consistently show that he is deeply unpopular, matching or exceeding his own past lows in many opinion surveys. Republicans look likely to lose the House and perhaps also the Senate in this fall’s elections, and more Democratic power in Washington would make Trump’s life more difficult. As for the endorsements, the record is clear. My colleague Will Gottsegen noted last week that most Trump-backed candidates still win, but he’s had some notable misses as well.

Not only is the reporting that infuriates Trump accurate, but siccing the FCC on it makes no legal sense. The agency regulates radio and TV outlets, but much polling is conducted by print outlets and other organizations. The FCC doesn’t have any authority to punish NBC News for reporting on things the president doesn’t like, whether accurate or not. The FCC’s site states (for now) that intervening in such cases “would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.” If the FCC or any other federal agency can do that, freedom of the press no longer exists.

But Trump doesn’t care about this bedrock civil liberty. He’s tried to wield the FCC as a political tool, and he’s been helped by its chair, Brendan Carr, a Project 2025 co-author who has advocated for the use of regulatory agencies as partisan hatchet men. Just because the FCC doesn’t have the power doesn’t mean that Carr won’t try. Before Trump was president, MAGA figures complained about what they saw as “jawboning,” when government officials found informal ways to pressure companies; now they are enthusiastic about the practice. Carr has had some success bullying major outlets, though companies have recently been finding strength to resist.

Trump has also attempted to silence the press via lawsuits. He has sued ABC, CBS, The New York Times, the Des Moines Register, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal, the pollster J. Ann Selzer, the Pulitzer Prize Board, and the journalist Bob Woodward. Some defendants have settled; other suits have failed, and still more remain in process. Last week, Trump updated an absurd defamation case against the Times. Part of the goal is intimidation. Huge papers with strong legal departments such as the Times and Journal may not blanch before such lawsuits, but smaller outlets might think twice about what they publish. (Trump’s FBI director, Kash Patel, also recently filed a lawsuit against The Atlantic, demanding $250 million, in response to reporting he did not like. The Atlantic has filed a motion to dismiss, along with a request to begin seeking factual discovery from the FBI and the Department of Justice. “If Director Patel did not want to face this process, he should not have filed this suit,” The Atlantic’s editor in chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, has said.)

The attitude from the president permeates the rest of his administration. The finance ministers of the G20 are meeting today in Asheville, North Carolina, but the Treasury Department barred specific reporters from the Times, Journal, and Bloomberg News. The reasons these reporters were singled out is not clear. The Treasury Department noted that a wide range of outlets had been credentialed for the event but declined to discuss the specific cases on the record. The United States won’t have much credibility to criticize crackdowns on the press in, say, China or Russia (both attendees), but then again, this administration probably wouldn’t bother. As the National Press Club said in a statement, “When government officials decide which journalists may enter the room, they begin to control which questions get asked, whose scrutiny they face and what the public gets to see and hear.”

The situation is even bleaker at the Department of Defense. The Washington Post yesterday reported that top military leaders have warned Secretary Pete Hegseth that extending the war in Iran “is unsustainable and risks weakening their ability to confront threats elsewhere, including the U.S. homeland.” The reaction from the Pentagon, which has consistently tried to limit and hide information about the floundering war, was furious. One can understand why the department is, well, defensive: Failed and failing military operations have brought down administrations before.

The Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell claimed that the report was “inaccurate” and added that “publishing highly classified assessments from the Secretary’s orders book is a crime.” That allegation is, itself, broadly misleading and arguably just false. But MAGA supporters outside the administration eagerly agreed. The Trump ally and Post columnist Marc Thiessen, who keeps insisting that the war is going swimmingly, criticized the leak that his own paper received. (Pro tip: If you’re not willing to stand for transparency, journalism is the wrong line of work.)

These are the latest steps in a clampdown at the Defense Department. The Pentagon is trying to turn Stars and Stripes, a venerable military newspaper, into a propaganda outlet. (Firings there are paused during litigation.) Whether it makes sense for a government agency to house an independent publication is open for debate, but what’s clear is that Trump officials are targeting Stars and Stripes because of unflattering reporting—including on conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln—that is truthful and relevant to the public and troops.

Under Hegseth, the department has drastically reduced press access at the Pentagon and, as the Post also reported yesterday, begun hiring right-wing influencers. Despite these efforts, the Iran war is deeply unpopular, and as the Post stories demonstrate, traditional outlets continue to report with depth, rigor, and accuracy on the administration’s actions. This should be a warning for the enemies of free speech who run the federal government: Targeting the press isn’t just un-American; it also doesn’t work.

We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys

After reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, I have a new destination for a time machine, should I ever finally get my hands on one. I’d set the dial to some night in the late 1970s or ’80s and visit the boyhood rooms of the Silicon Valley titans Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, and Sam Altman.
